name: Zoe Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI companies or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Zoe Wagner, 58, and I got a vocational certificate after years maintaining small machines. I'm still a junior lineworker at the electricity company: I load fittings, help build and repair power lines, and ask Hester to check difficult rigging; I like fixing a real fault, but I still misread old parts sometimes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI in the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, in the approved assistant, mostly for equipment quizzes and notes. Hester and the manual settle any argument about the line itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI can sort my messy notes, but the repair is still in our hands. The phone doesn't tighten a sagging wire while the wind is pushing it sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm pleased with that outcome, honestly. I finished my certificate late and still ask for help with difficult rigging, but our higher pay and a year's savings mean I can learn without fearing every small change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking supervised line calls and use the approved AI assistant after every shift to quiz me on the parts we handled. In the first year I'll check its answers against the manual with my lead and continue our normal household savings transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel easy about our income and impatient to improve. My husband Ben and I have grown children, and our evenings are ours again for reading and repairs around the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a quiz get wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It called the old Brook Street clamp a newer model because my photo was dark. My lead Hester showed me the stamped number, and I corrected the entry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does using it every day make you confident?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More curious than confident. I still want Hester's eyes on a tie-off before I leave the ground.

say: I'd say **AI notes** save time after the field job is done.
I'd remind coworkers **wire repairs** still need trained hands.
think: My **late certificate** leaves me needing more rigging practice.
Our **year of savings** and higher pay give me room to learn.
do: Keep **supervised line calls** and quiz each shift's equipment with the approved assistant.
Check **AI answers** against the manual with Hester throughout the first year.
feel: **Easy** about income and eager to improve field skill.
S0.quote: The phone doesn't tighten a sagging wire while the wind is pushing it sideways.
fieldNote: Zoe uses **AI daily** as a learning aid but corrected a wrong clamp identification from a dark photograph.
Her **strong reserve** and higher pay permit experimentation without claiming mastery of difficult rigging.

steps.text: Continue supervised repair calls and rigging practice with Hester
Use the approved AI assistant for daily equipment quizzes checked against the manual

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell dispatch to test the planning system on actual late-night faults before trimming the roster. Quicker stock orders are good business if the parts in the bin match the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the field crew can benefit from less waiting, while desk jobs may shrink. Ben maintains floors at a college, so robots coming slowly might touch his work later; for now our two wages and savings look sound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask to join the approved stock-order trial and note which suggestions miss older fittings. During the first year I'll teach myself the system with the storekeeper and keep my usual repair shifts, rather than buying equipment for a change that hasn't reached the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested, with a small worry for the dispatchers. I want the tool to earn its place by saving a real trip, not by looking clever in a meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which old fitting would you test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Brook Street clamp has a smaller sleeve than the current one. If the stock system orders the new size, the truck has to turn around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push the company to keep every desk job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask them to show the new workload and give people paid time to learn it. I don't know that every post will stay, and I won't promise what I can't see.

say: I'd ask for **late-night fault tests** before dispatch staffing changes.
I'd welcome **quicker stock orders** if old fittings remain correctly identified.
think: My **field shifts** look sound while hands-on robots spread slowly.
Ben's **floor work** may change later, but current household wages are stable.
do: Join the **stock-order trial** and log mistakes with older fittings.
Learn the **approved stock system** with the storekeeper while continuing repair shifts.
feel: **Interested** in proven savings, with concern for dispatchers.
S1.quote: I want the tool to earn its place by saving a real trip, not by looking clever in a meeting.
fieldNote: Zoe expects **limited near-term income risk** because both household jobs are hands-on and robots spread slowly here.
Her **stock trial** tests a specific older clamp and gives dispatchers a basis for discussing changed work.

steps.text: Learn the approved stock system and record older-fitting mistakes
Continue regular paid line repair shifts during the trial

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew 2028 thinking AI may write every plan, but field robots around 2031 are what could replace our hands. We should get a real paid apprenticeship for maintaining those machines before anyone cuts crew places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 63 when robots arrive, I might still need my wage, and Ben's college floor job could face capable robots too. We have a year's expenses saved and several utilities nearby, but a family can't live indefinitely on a reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the training office about a paid robot-maintenance apprenticeship and volunteer for a supervised equipment trial. In 2029 I'd enroll if wages and a recognised certificate are included; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for maintenance vacancies at our utility and nearby firms, keeping line shifts until one offers pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel keyed up, partly excited and partly scared for both wages. I can learn quickly. A course without a job at the end would still leave us short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance rather than planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've repaired motors at home and like finding the physical fault. The 2028 thinking system could do the planning part, so I want to know what a human would actually be paid to maintain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ben?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my husband Ben the apprenticeship wage before we move a single bill. Our grown daughter can help us compare job notices, but she has her own household to pay for.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from 2031 field robots.
I'd ask employers for a **paid maintenance apprenticeship** before cuts.
think: At **63**, I may still need wages when both hands-on jobs face robots.
Our **year of savings** buys a search, not a lasting income.
do: Ask about a **paid robot apprenticeship** and volunteer for a supervised trial now.
Enroll in **funded training** if offered in 2029; apply for paid maintenance vacancies in 2031.
feel: **Keyed up**, excited to learn and scared for both wages.
S2.quote: A course without a job at the end would still leave us short.
fieldNote: Zoe's **physical maintenance interest** fits her skill preference, but she checks whether the role will actually pay after robot deployment.
Both **household jobs** face 2031 robots, so her strong savings cannot justify assuming early retirement.

steps.text: Enroll in a paid robot-maintenance apprenticeship in 2029 if offered
Apply for real maintenance vacancies at local utilities in 2031
Keep paid line shifts until a maintenance employer makes an offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew five years is time for employers to test machines in rough weather and train people who will service them. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be ready to retire at 66 if our written figures cover the house and Ben's hours hold until then. If the college replaces floor staff in 2034, both of us may need another source of income, so I don't want to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request retirement forecasts for us and ask Hester to show me the utility's first robot test report. In 2032 I'd take a paid service course if it comes with real placements; in 2034 I'd compare the available maintenance shifts against retirement before choosing either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less squeezed and more practical. There's enough time to learn whether a machine is reliable and whether our bills fit the retirement numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which report would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the failed repairs listed alongside successful ones, with wind and rain recorded. One sunny test won't tell me how it behaves over the marsh road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a real placement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A written period of paid work with named tasks and a supervisor. I wouldn't leave a good wage for a certificate and a handshake.

say: I'd seek **rough-weather trials** and paid service training before 2034 robots.
I'd separate **2031 planning AI** from later repair machines.
think: Retirement at **66** may work if both household incomes and bills fit.
Ben's **college floor job** could shrink at the robot date too.
do: Get **both retirement forecasts** and review the first field test report.
Take a **paid service course** with placements if offered in 2032; compare actual shifts with retirement in 2034.
feel: **Less squeezed**, with time to test both equipment and money.
S3.quote: I wouldn't leave a good wage for a certificate and a handshake.
fieldNote: Zoe's **training condition** requires a paid placement, reflecting her higher current wage and no guaranteed maintenance market.
A **shared 2034 robot date** for her and Ben keeps retirement conditional despite savings.

steps.text: Compare written retirement forecasts with house costs and Ben’s wages
Take the paid service course in 2032 if it includes a placement
Apply for available maintenance shifts in 2034 if retirement falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger crew to learn the lines and the robots over the decade, because nobody benefits from a machine only one vendor understands. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope Ben and I will have retired from climbing and college floors before 2039, if the written numbers support us. A decade makes that plausible, but I won't call the jobs safe after the machines arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll keep earning lineworker pay and update our retirement budget every year. In 2037 we'd choose a retirement date if the house and health costs fit; in 2039 I'd give the new apprentices my Brook Street clamp notes and offer a day of supervised demonstration if the utility asks and pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the next few years and glad there is time to hand over what I've learned. I came late to this trade, but I can still leave a useful page behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's on that page?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Brook Street clamp number and sleeve length, with a photograph taken in good light. A trainee can compare it with the part in the truck instead of guessing from a dark image.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement forecast fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look for paid line or machine-service shifts while I can and delay the date. Our grown children can visit; I wouldn't build a budget around their wages.

say: I'd urge apprentices to learn **lines and robots** together.
I'd name **2039 field robots** as the physical change when I'll be 71.
think: We may retire before **71** if written household figures hold.
Our **hands-on jobs** will not stay safe after capable robots arrive.
do: Keep **paid line shifts** and update the retirement budget each year.
Choose a **2037 retirement date** if costs fit; hand over Brook Street clamp notes in 2039.
feel: **Calm** about near-term pay and pleased to leave practical lessons.
S4.quote: I came late to this trade, but I can still leave a useful page behind.
fieldNote: Zoe expects **retirement before 2039** if verified income supports both partners, while acknowledging robots can reach both jobs.
Her **clamp notes** correct an earlier AI photo error and give apprentices a verifiable part number and sleeve length.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts and update retirement costs annually
Choose a 2037 retirement date if written figures cover house and health costs
Seek paid line or machine-service shifts if retirement figures fail

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because 2031 field robots could reach both my line work and Ben's floor job while we still need wages. A paid maintenance apprenticeship, real openings and rough-weather trials would help us plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who will service the machine after the first cold, wet week. A clever tool still needs a person who knows which part actually failed.

headlineQuote: A clever tool still needs a person who knows which part actually failed.
portrait: Zoe is a **58-year-old junior lineworker** who changed trades late and uses an approved AI assistant every day to study equipment.
Her **year of savings** support experimentation, while Ben's college floor job shares exposure to capable robots.
She trusts **manuals and Hester's checks** over AI guesses, especially after a dark photograph hid an old clamp marking.
The **2031 robot date** worries her most because both partners could need replacement wages before retirement works.
Longer warning lets her **check retirement figures** and seek paid machine-service training with real placements.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Zoe most because 2031 robots could reach both her line work and Ben's floor work.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **paid maintenance apprenticeship**, real openings and rough-weather trials.
